conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this sharp pain in my upper belly again—same as always. It started two days ago. I’ve also been nauseous and throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is the pain different from your usual pain, or is it the same pattern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s identical. Mid-epigastric, sharp. Nothing makes it better or worse. I’ve also had diarrhea this time, which happens sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how have your blood sugars been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really high. I haven’t been taking my insulin for about a week. I feel more energetic without it, honestly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand that, but going without insulin is very dangerous. Your blood sugar was over 400 in the ER. That can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis, coma, or even death.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I just don’t like how I feel when I take it. Sluggish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But we need to keep you safe. You got 10 units of insulin in the ER, and your levels are starting to stabilize. We’ll help you manage this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I don’t want to be here long. I just want the pain treated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain, but we also have to treat the high blood sugar. You’re in diabetic ketoacidosis, which means your body is producing dangerous acids. Insulin fixes that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I have to take insulin now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll give it by injection. You’re on a sliding scale for now, and we’ll restart your long-acting insulin at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Whatever. Can I get something for the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re already on Dilaudid 2mg every 3 hours as needed. You can have a dose now if you’re in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it. I’m in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll order it now. We also checked your labs. Your pancreas enzymes are elevated, which fits with your chronic pancreatitis flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not something new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks like your usual pattern. No signs of infection or blockage. Your last gastric emptying study was normal, so we don’t think gastroparesis is causing the nausea this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I hate being told it’s all in my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not. Your pain is real, and we’re treating it. But we also need to address the insulin. Can we talk about why you stopped taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel better without it. More awake. I know it’s risky, but I’ve done it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but each time you do this, you risk serious complications. We’ll work with your PCP to support you, but you must take your insulin to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. I’ll take it when I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a start. We’ll make sure you have your prescriptions and know how to use them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Just checking in. How’s the pain and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s a little better. Haven’t thrown up since yesterday. Still feel shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is coming down—273 now. That’s much better. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat something? I’m hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can try a regular diabetic diet. Start small and see how you do. No nausea is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well overnight. You ate dinner and breakfast without any nausea or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel okay. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. Your blood sugar is stable, you’re tolerating food, and your pain is controlled with your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t like being here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But before you go, we need to talk about your insulin. You agreed to restart it. Do you have any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. I’ll take it. But I don’t like it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. Just know it’s life-saving. Call your doctor if you have concerns. Also, keep using your Dilaudid as prescribed—only for severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know how to manage my pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you do. We just want to keep things safe and consistent. You’ll follow up with your PCP soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have an appointment next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll send all the records. You’re cleared to go home. Someone will bring your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before you leave. Any pain or nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m fine. Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember: take your Lantus every night. If you skip it, you could end up back here with ketoacidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it. I don’t want to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And call your doctor if your pain changes or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.
